newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan scandal could benefit foreign brokers.
newsitem.headline: Japan scandal could benefit foreign brokers.

text.p: A high-profile scandal at giant brokerage Nomura Securities Co Ltd could give a boost to efforts by foreign brokerages to gain market share in Japan.
But basically, foreign brokers are counting on structural changes in the market and their ability to meet clients' needs -- not scandal fallout -- to help them grab more business.
"At the margin, clearly some business is coming in from people who don't want to do business with Nomura," said John Baldwin, general manager of Jardine Fleming Securities Ltd's Tokyo branch.
"But the scandal is only one of many things," Baldwin said. "Medium-term, other structural forces continue to benefit foreigners."

Former Nomura president Hideo Sakamaki was arrested last Friday on suspicion of conspiring with three Nomura executives to pay 38.5 million yen ($331,000) in 1995 to Ryuichi Koike, a "sokaiya" corporate racketeer at the heart of the affair.
Sokaiya buy shares in firms and extort money by threatening to disrupt shareholders' meetings. Paying them off is illegal.

Sakamaki's arrest, which followed the arrests of three other Nomura executives, as well as Ryuichi Koike and his younger brother Yoshinori earlier in May, has further dented Nomura's credibility and looks likely to foreshadow stern punishment for the brokerage, now enmeshed in its second scandal in six years.
The scandal coincides with rising prominence of foreign brokerages in Tokyo and expectations that their presence will expand as Japan implements its "Big Bang" financial reforms.
Japan aims to liberalise its financial markets by 2001 to catch up with reforms carried out more than a decade ago in Europe and North America.

Three foreign brokerages -- Merrill Lynch Japan Inc, Morgan Stanley Japan Ltd and Goldman Sachs (Japan) Ltd -- placed among the top 10 firms in terms of share of equities turnover on the Tokyo Stock Exchange (TSE) both in February, before the scandal hit front pages, and in April after it grabbed the headlines, financial daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun reported this week.
"There is a myth of the impenetrability of Japan's financial markets, but actually, 'gaijin' (foreigners) are doing quite all right, thank you," said one foreign analyst.
Japan's Big Four Brokerages -- Nomura, Daiwa Securities Co Ltd, Nikko Securities Co Ltd and Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd -- accounted for about one-third of the turnover in both months.
But Nomura slid to fourth place with 6.26 percent of TSE share turnover in April from top place with 11.38 percent in February and languished at third with 6.4 percent in May.
How long customers will stay away once official punishment for Nomura, expected to be harsh, is meted out is uncertain.

"Some clients are saying they still value Nomura's research capability and their timely and high-quality service, so some will probably go back," said Naoko Nemoto, a brokerage analyst at rating agency Standard & Poor's Corp (S&P).

"But we are increasingly suspicious about how loyal they are. Probably if they are ordered to suspend (some business) for up to six months and some investors find they can do without Nomura, the impact will be more permanent," she added.

Some in the industry, however, say Nomura could emerge even stronger from the scandal crucible and many agree the brokerage should by no means be crossed off as a future winner as Japan proceeds with deregulation of its financial markets.

"You could argue this will provide the stimulus Nomura needs to get sorted out and come back with tremendous strength," said Patrick Murray, Tokyo branch manager at HSBC James Capel. "For a foreign house to say it's time to...compete head-on with Nomura is extremely dangerous."

Scandals aside, foreign brokerages -- especially Nomura's U.S. rivals -- are clearly ambitious. "There isn't a single major American brokerage out there that doesn't want to beat Nomura," the foreign analyst said.
"The scandal itself is not going to be the reason why Nomura or any Japanese company will be beaten by American companies. It may, however, be a catalyst," he said.
Foreign brokers generally hope Tokyo's Big Bang reforms will give them an edge as competition focuses more on products and service rather than "old boy" personal and corporate ties.

"For customers, one key point will be information, so brokerages like us intend to compete based on our research capability and other value-added aspects..." said Sumiko Iwadate, a spokeswoman for Morgan Stanley Japan Ltd.
Home-grown brokerages may have more trouble adapting to the new post-Big Bang environment, Jardine Fleming's Baldwin said.

"The less strict regulatory environment will gradually mean that Nomura as well as the other big (Japanese) brokerages have problems," Baldwin said. "I think that many are operating on the basis of old paradigms."
